questions.stem: (a) In the feudal system introduced into England after 1066, who in theory owned all the land? (b) What name was given to unfree peasants who owed their lord unpaid labour and could not leave their village without permission?
markscheme: B1: (a) the king
B1: (b) serfs (accept villeins)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) The king. After the Norman Conquest, William the Conqueror claimed ownership of all the land and granted estates (fiefs) to his barons in return for loyalty and military service. (b) Serfs, also called villeins — peasants bound to their lord's manor who owed several days of unpaid labour each week on the lord's own land and needed his permission to leave the village.

questions.stem: (a) In which year did 'Bloody Sunday' take place in St Petersburg? (b) What had the peaceful marchers, led by Father Gapon, come to the Winter Palace to do?
markscheme: B1: to present (hand in) a petition to the Tsar asking for reforms
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Bloody Sunday happened in January 1905. (b) The crowd of workers, led by the priest Father Gapon, had marched to the Winter Palace to present a petition to Tsar Nicholas II asking for reforms. Troops opened fire, killing or wounding hundreds; the massacre destroyed the belief in the Tsar as the people's caring 'Little Father' and set off the 1905 revolution.

questions.stem: (a) What did the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 take away from Jewish Germans? (b) Name the organised, nationwide attack on Jewish shops, homes and synagogues in November 1938.
markscheme: B1: their German citizenship (with marriage between Jews and non-Jews also banned)
B1: Kristallnacht (the 'Night of Broken Glass')
questions.modelAnswer: (a) The Nuremberg Laws stripped Jewish Germans of their German citizenship and banned marriages between Jews and non-Jews, defining who counted as Jewish by ancestry. (b) The November 1938 pogrom was Kristallnacht, the 'Night of Broken Glass', in which synagogues were burned, shops and homes smashed, about 100 people killed and 30,000 Jewish men sent to concentration camps.

questions.stem: The Great Wall of China was never simply a military barrier. Give THREE purposes or effects of the Wall besides defending against nomadic raids.
markscheme: B1: it marked the boundary of the settled farming world (the edge of the Chinese world)
B1: it channelled trade through controlled gates, where goods could be checked and taxed
B1: it served as a symbol of imperial power — and of the immense human effort and suffering it cost
questions.modelAnswer: The Great Wall guarded the northern frontier, but it did much more. It marked the boundary between the settled farming world and the steppe beyond; it channelled trade through controlled gates, letting the empire monitor and tax goods; and it stood as a vast symbol of imperial power — and of the immense human effort and suffering it cost, since conscripted labourers died in huge numbers building it. The Wall was also never impenetrable: determined invaders such as the Mongols bribed guards or simply rode around it.

questions.stem: Explain how the Second World War helped to bring about Indian independence in 1947.
markscheme: B1: by 1945 Britain was exhausted and nearly bankrupt, and the new Labour government wanted to leave India
B1: over two million Indian soldiers had volunteered to fight, strengthening the expectation that India had earned freedom
B1: Britain could no longer rely on Indian forces to hold India down, as the 1946 Royal Indian Navy mutiny showed
questions.modelAnswer: The war broke both Britain's ability and its will to keep India. By 1945 Britain was exhausted and nearly bankrupt, and the new Labour government wanted to leave. More than two million Indian soldiers had volunteered to fight — the largest volunteer army in history — and many expected freedom in return, while Congress's Quit India campaign of 1942 had shown the depth of opposition. Finally, the Royal Indian Navy mutiny of 1946 showed that Britain could no longer rely on Indian forces to hold the country down. After 1945, independence was a question of how, not whether.

questions.stem: Give TWO reasons why the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 failed to achieve its long-term aim of knocking the United States out of the Pacific.
markscheme: B1: the crucial US aircraft carriers were at sea and survived the attack
B1: the base's fuel tanks and repair yards were left untouched (accept: the attack united the American people in determination to fight)
questions.modelAnswer: First, the US aircraft carriers — the decisive weapon of the Pacific War — were at sea during the attack and survived. Second, Pearl Harbor's fuel tanks and repair yards were left untouched, so the Pacific Fleet could recover quickly. Worse still for Japan, the surprise attack enraged and united the American people; far from forcing the USA to negotiate, it brought America's enormous industrial power fully into the war.

questions.stem: Source A: an extract from a letter home by Private T. Marlow, a fictional British soldier on the Western Front, written in October 1916. "The rain has not stopped for a week and the trench is a river of mud. Last night we stood in water up to our ankles, and my boots have not been dry since Tuesday. Rats bigger than cats run over us as we sleep. This morning the guns opened up again — the noise is like the end of the world, and when it stops the silence frightens you more. We go over the top at dawn." What can you learn from Source A about conditions in the trenches? Make THREE supported points, using a quotation for each.
markscheme: B1: valid point about the physical misery of mud and water, e.g. "a river of mud" or "water up to our ankles"
B1: valid point about vermin and daily discomfort, e.g. "Rats bigger than cats run over us as we sleep"
B1: valid point about fear and psychological strain, e.g. "the silence frightens you more" or "We go over the top at dawn"
questions.modelAnswer: The letter shows, first, the physical misery: rain turned the trench into "a river of mud" and men stood in "water up to our ankles" with wet boots for days — conditions that caused trench foot. Second, it shows the filth and vermin soldiers lived with: "Rats bigger than cats run over us as we sleep". Third, it reveals the psychological strain of trench warfare: the noise of the guns "is like the end of the world", yet when it stops "the silence frightens you more", and the closing line "We go over the top at dawn" hints at the dread of the coming attack.

questions.stem: "Without the Great Depression, Hitler would never have become Chancellor in 1933." How far do you agree with this statement? Give reasons for your judgement.
markscheme: B1: evidence supporting the statement, e.g. the Depression pushed unemployment past 6 million and Nazi seats soared from 12 (1928) to 230 (July 1932)
B1: evidence of other causes, e.g. Nazi propaganda and SA violence / hatred of Versailles / the back-room deal by von Papen and Hindenburg
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. the Depression created the despair the Nazis exploited, but Hitler still needed elite backing to take power
questions.modelAnswer: The evidence strongly supports the statement: in the prosperous years the Nazis won just 12 Reichstag seats in 1928, but as the Depression drove unemployment past six million their vote exploded to 230 seats by July 1932 — economic despair drove voters towards extremist promises of jobs and order, and destroyed faith in Weimar democracy. However, the Depression alone did not make Hitler Chancellor: the Nazis never won a majority, and Hitler gained power in January 1933 only because conservative politicians such as von Papen persuaded President Hindenburg to appoint him, arrogantly believing they could control him. On balance, the Depression was the essential precondition — without it the Nazis would have remained a fringe party — but the back-room deal was the final step.
